text: Okay, let’s actually do it. Copy a big model’s thinking into a small one.
Our student is Qwen, the real half-a-billion-parameter model. Tiny’s big sibling.
We’ll show it about a thousand worked answers, on a free GPU, in under an hour.
That sounds almost too easy.
Here’s the twist to watch for. A student often learns to sound like the teacher, before it learns to think like it.
Copying a big model’s thinking. Episode two.
We open a free dataset of worked answers, written in the style of DeepSeek R1. About seven and a half thousand school maths problems.
Do we just trust it?
Never. Read some first. In the first hundred rows, ninety-seven were marked correct, and they all matched the real answers.
But look at the length. Problems a person solves in three lines get a whole page of thinking.
Keep an eye on that. It’ll matter later.
Step one: rewrite each answer into our format. We keep the thinking.
But the teacher writes its final answer in a box, inside a sentence.
So we pull out the number, and rebuild the reply with our answer tags.
Same habit everywhere: think, then answer.
Step two: a free GPU can’t handle huge answers, so we drop anything over a thousand and twenty-four tokens, and keep the first thousand.
The long ones are too big. Out they go.
Wait. So we only keep the teacher’s shorter answers?
Exactly. What you filter is what you teach.
The student copies style as well as skill. By picking shorter answers, we’re teaching it to be more concise.
Step three: measure before you train. Always.
Like a before photo.
Right. Then we train, and measure again.
On the same two hundred test problems, which the student has never seen, always picking its most likely answer, so nothing is luck.
Three numbers: accuracy, format, and tokens. Is it right, does it use the tags, and how long does it think?
Step four, training. Instead of rewriting all five hundred million weights, we add sticky notes. That’s LoRA.
Like scribbling in the margins of a textbook, instead of reprinting it.
Exactly. And the student is only graded on the teacher’s reply, not on copying the question back.
One more detail: the free GPU needs sixteen-bit numbers of the older kind. The script switches for you.
Training’s done. Of our three numbers, which one usually changes first?
Pause, and have a guess.
A! It copied a much smarter model, so it should just get smarter.
That’s the hope. But usually it’s B. Format and length.
Here’s how to read your table.
Format jumps to nearly a hundred percent? It learned the layout from the teacher.
Tokens jump a lot? It copied the teacher’s long thinking style.
Accuracy rises? The copied reasoning is actually helping.
And if accuracy stays flat, but the answers got way longer?
Then it copied the style, more than the skill. Accuracy is the honest measure.
Then read at least three replies yourself. Does the student say wait, let me check?
A real check recomputes a step.
An empty one just says the words, and changes nothing.
Ha. So it’s a parrot. It learned the catchphrase!
Sometimes. So find one problem it used to get right, and now gets wrong, and ask why. That’s the most useful thing in this lab.
Quick recap.
You don’t need the teacher running. Just its saved answers.
What you filter is what you teach, including length.
And measure before and after. Trust accuracy, then read the replies.
And that’s every tool in the box. Rewards, GRPO, curves, shorter thinking, and copying.
